extended_definition: The most common Hebrew word for God. Plural in form but singular in meaning when referring to the God of Israel, expressing fullness, majesty, and power. Used over 2,600 times in the Old Testament. First appears in Genesis 1:1.

definition: The LORD, the personal name of God
extended_definition: The covenant name of God, often written as LORD in English translations. Derived from the verb 'to be' (havah), signifying the eternal, self-existent nature of God. Revealed to Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3:14). The most frequent name for God in the OT with over 6,800 occurrences.

The basic Hebrew word for God, emphasizing strength and power. Used as a component of many names (El Shaddai, El Elyon) and personal names (Elijah, Elisha, Israel). Points to God as the source of all power and authority.

A name of God often translated 'Almighty.' Frequently paired with El (God Almighty). Used especially in the patriarchal narratives and Job. Possibly derived from a root meaning 'mountain' or 'sufficient,' portraying God as the all-sufficient provider and sustainer.

A title meaning 'my Lord' or 'my Master,' used as a reverent substitute for YHWH in Jewish tradition. Emphasizes God's authority and lordship over all creation. Used by Abraham when interceding for Sodom (Genesis 18:27).

One of the richest theological words in Hebrew, hesed describes covenantal love that is faithful, loyal, and enduring. It combines love with loyalty and action. Often translated 'steadfast love' in modern versions, it is central to God's character (Exodus 34:6-7) and forms the basis of his covenant relationship with Israel.

definition: To love, to like, to delight in
extended_definition: The most common Hebrew word for love, used of both human and divine affection. Used of God's love for Israel (Deuteronomy 7:8) and of the greatest commandment to love God (Deuteronomy 6:5). Also describes love between people, family affection, and friendship.

Far richer than the English 'peace,' shalom describes a state of total well-being — harmony with God, others, and creation. It encompasses physical health, prosperity, safety, and right relationships. God is called the 'God of shalom' and it is his gift to his people. Used as a greeting and blessing in Jewish culture.

Derived from the root 'aman' (to be firm, reliable), emunah describes trustworthiness and reliability. In Habakkuk 2:4 — 'the righteous shall live by his faithfulness' — it is the foundation of Paul's teaching on justification by faith. It emphasizes active, lived faithfulness rather than mere belief.

definition: To trust, to be confident, to rely on
extended_definition: Describes a confident reliance and security that comes from resting in someone or something. Used repeatedly in the Psalms for trusting in God (Psalm 37:3-5). Conveys the idea of leaning one's weight on, or feeling safe under the care of. The opposite of fear and anxiety.

Literally a 'cord' or 'thread,' tiqvah came to mean hope as a line stretched toward the future. The same word is used of Rahab's scarlet cord (Joshua 2:18) that signified her salvation. Hope in the Old Testament is always grounded in God's faithfulness and promises.

definition: Soul, life, living being, breath, person
extended_definition: One of the most theologically significant Hebrew words, nephesh refers to the whole living being — body and breath together. It does not describe an immortal soul separate from the body but the entirety of a living person. God breathed nephesh into Adam (Genesis 2:7). Used of humans, animals, and even God's own being.

A fundamental Hebrew word with a range of meanings: the physical wind, the breath of life, and the Spirit of God. The Ruach Elohim (Spirit of God) hovered over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2). It is the animating power of life and the vehicle of God's presence and action in the world.

definition: Heart, mind, inner man, will, understanding
extended_definition: In Hebrew thought, the heart is the center of the entire person — intellect, will, emotion, and moral life. It is not primarily the seat of emotions (as in modern usage) but of thought and decision-making. The greatest commandment calls for loving God with all one's heart (Deuteronomy 6:5). God searches the heart (Jeremiah 17:10).

Rooted in 'aman' (to be firm), emet describes that which is solid, reliable, and trustworthy. God's word is emet (Psalm 119:160). Often paired with hesed (steadfast love) to describe God's character. In rabbinic tradition, emet is the seal of God. It points to objective reality and not just subjective sincerity.

Describes conformity to a standard — specifically God's standard of right relationship and right action. Not merely moral uprightness, but includes justice for the poor and oppressed. Abraham's faith was credited to him as tsedaqah (Genesis 15:6). God's own righteousness is the standard by which all is measured.

Refers to the act of judging, the verdict rendered, and the standard by which it is rendered. Mishpat includes both the process of justice and its content — fair treatment, especially for the weak and vulnerable. Micah 6:8 calls Israel to 'do mishpat.' God himself is the perfect judge who executes mishpat.

Describes that which is separated from the common and dedicated to God. The fundamental meaning is 'to be set apart.' God alone is intrinsically holy (Isaiah 6:3), and persons, places, and objects become holy by association with him. Israel is called to be a holy nation (Exodus 19:6).

From a root meaning 'to be heavy or weighty,' kabod denotes that which has substance and importance. The glory of God is his visible, weighty presence — light, fire, and majesty that fills the tabernacle and temple. It describes the honor, fame, and importance that belongs rightly to God and that he shares with his people.

The root of 'hallelujah' (praise the LORD). Halal means to boast or make a show, often in a joyful and exuberant way. It points to praise that is enthusiastic and public. The Psalms are filled with calls to halal the LORD. True praise is a response to who God is, not merely to what he does.

definition: To bow down, worship, prostrate oneself
extended_definition: The primary OT word for worship, literally meaning to fall down or prostrate oneself. It conveys complete submission and homage before God or a king. True worship in Scripture involves the posture of the whole person — physical, emotional, and spiritual — bowing in acknowledgment of God's supremacy.

The covenant is the central organizing concept of the entire Bible. Berith refers to a solemn, binding agreement — often ratified with sacrifice, oaths, and signs. God establishes covenants with Noah, Abraham, Israel at Sinai, David, and finally the new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31-34). Each covenant reveals more of God's redemptive plan.

From the root yasha (to save, deliver), yeshuah is the word behind the name Jesus (Yeshua). It describes God's rescuing action — freeing from enemies, sin, and death. First used in Jacob's blessing (Genesis 49:18). It encompasses not just future forgiveness but present wholeness and victory.

The central sacrificial term in the Old Testament, describing the covering or wiping away of sin. The Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur) takes its name from this word. Kaphar involves a substitutionary covering — the blood of sacrifice covers the guilt of the sinner. It points forward to Christ's ultimate atonement.

definition: To sin, miss the mark, go wrong
extended_definition: The primary word for sin, originally an archery term meaning to miss the target. It captures the nature of sin as falling short of God's standard rather than just willful rebellion. Used of unintentional as well as deliberate failures. The sacrificial system addresses chata through atonement.

The strongest Hebrew word for sin, describing deliberate rebellion and defiance against authority. Unlike chata (missing the mark), pesha is willful and relational — a breaking away from covenant with God. Isaiah 53 uses this word for what the Servant of the LORD bears on behalf of his people.

Often translated 'law,' torah is better understood as 'instruction' or 'teaching.' It comes from a root meaning 'to direct or point the way.' The Torah is not merely a legal code but God's loving instruction for his covenant people. Psalm 119 celebrates the beauty and gift of Torah in 176 verses.

Biblical wisdom is not merely intellectual knowledge but the skill of living rightly before God. It begins with the fear of the LORD (Proverbs 1:7). Chokmah is applied wisdom — the ability to make right choices in concrete situations. God is the source of all wisdom, and it is a gift to those who ask (James 1:5 echoes this).

The Hebrew 'word' (dabar) is not merely a sound but an active event — God's dabar accomplishes what he sends it to do (Isaiah 55:11). It encompasses the spoken word, a matter or affair, and a promise. The Ten Commandments are literally the 'Ten Words' (Devarim). Dabar is powerful and creative.

Refers to a long and undefined stretch of time — often translated 'forever' or 'everlasting.' When used of God, it expresses his eternal nature. God's hesed is described as olam (Psalm 136). It can refer to ancient times past or the indefinite future. The 'everlasting covenant' (berith olam) is central to Israel's hope.

definition: To know, to perceive, to understand, to experience
extended_definition: Hebrew 'knowing' is relational and experiential, not merely intellectual. To know God (yada Elohim) is to have a personal, covenant relationship with him, not just factual knowledge about him. Adam 'knew' Eve — a deep, intimate knowing. Hosea laments Israel's lack of da'at (knowledge) of God (Hosea 4:6).

Literally means 'messenger' and can refer to human messengers, prophets, priests, or heavenly beings. The 'Angel of the LORD' (Malak YHWH) is a special figure in the OT who at times appears to represent God himself. Angels serve as God's agents in delivering messages, executing judgment, and protecting his people.

definition: To bless, to kneel, to praise
extended_definition: Comes from a root related to 'knee,' suggesting that blessing involves kneeling before God in reverence. God blesses his people (bestowing good), and his people bless God (acknowledging his goodness in worship). The Aaronic blessing (Numbers 6:24-26) is the primary barak text. Blessing flows from God to people and returns in worship.

The great Jewish confession (Deuteronomy 6:4) begins with 'Shema Israel' — 'Hear, O Israel.' In Hebrew, to truly hear means to obey — hearing and doing are inseparable. Shama expresses the covenantal responsiveness God desires from his people. Disobedience is described as 'not listening.'

The dominant OT word for repentance, literally meaning to turn around or return. The prophets constantly call Israel to shub — to turn back to the LORD. It involves a change of direction at the deepest level. Shub is both a turning from sin and a turning toward God. It is the heart of prophetic preaching.

The basic Hebrew word for king. God is described as the ultimate Melek — King of kings and Lord of lords. The tension between God's kingship and Israel's desire for a human king runs through 1 Samuel. The Psalms celebrate God as King (Psalms 47, 93, 95-99). The Messiah is the ultimate Davidic king.

Encompasses all aspects of life — physical vitality, the living God, and the water of life. God is described as 'the living God' (El Chay). The tree of life (ets ha-chayim) appears in both Genesis and Revelation. Life ultimately derives from God, who alone is the source of all chay.

Always in the plural, shamayim refers to the sky/atmosphere and the dwelling place of God. Genesis 1:1 begins 'In the beginning God created the heavens (shamayim) and the earth.' It is the realm of God's throne, of angels, and of the celestial bodies. Also used of the rain and 'the windows of heaven.'

One of the most frequently occurring Hebrew words, erets can refer to the whole earth, a specific land (like the land of Israel), or the ground. The promise of the land to Abraham's descendants is a key theological theme (erets as the Promised Land). It also represents God's creation that declares his glory.

definition: To wait, hope, expect, look eagerly
extended_definition: Qavah carries the idea of stretching toward something with eager expectation. Those who 'wait on the LORD' (qavah YHWH) will renew their strength (Isaiah 40:31). It is the active, expectant waiting that is the posture of faith — not passive resignation but eager anticipation of God's action.

The standard Greek word for God, used over 1,300 times in the New Testament. In John 1:1, the Word (Logos) is described as both 'with God' (ton theon) and 'God' (theos), a crucial theological distinction. Paul affirms that Christ is the fullness of the Godhead (Colossians 2:9). Theos always points to the one true God in NT usage.

The Greek translation of YHWH in the Septuagint, giving it enormous theological weight when applied to Jesus. 'Jesus is Lord' (Kurios Iesous) is the earliest Christian confession (Romans 10:9). Philippians 2:11 declares that every tongue will confess Jesus as Kurios. Applies also to God the Father and to human masters.

The Greek translation of the Hebrew Mashiach (Messiah), meaning 'anointed one.' In the OT, priests, prophets, and kings were anointed. Jesus fulfills all three offices. 'Christ' began as a title but quickly became inseparable from the name of Jesus. Central to the gospel: that Jesus is the long-awaited Messiah of Israel.

The Greek form of the Hebrew Yeshua (Joshua), meaning 'the LORD saves' or 'the LORD is salvation.' The angel instructed Joseph to name him Jesus 'because he will save his people from their sins' (Matthew 1:21). The name itself is a declaration of his mission. Every believer who calls on this name is saved (Romans 10:13).

The highest form of love in Greek — selfless, unconditional, and sacrificial. It is the word used in John 3:16 ('God so loved the world') and 1 Corinthians 13. Unlike eros (romantic love) or storge (family affection) or philia (friendship), agape loves without expecting anything in return. It is the defining characteristic of God's nature (1 John 4:8).

The central term in Paul's soteriology — justification is by faith (pistis), not works. Pistis encompasses mental assent, personal trust, and active reliance. In some texts, it refers to 'the faith' — the body of Christian belief (Jude 3). Hebrews 11:1 defines it: 'the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen.'

Christian hope (elpis) is not wishful thinking but confident expectation based on God's promises and Christ's resurrection. Romans 5 describes hope that 'does not disappoint.' The resurrection of Jesus is the anchor of Christian hope (1 Corinthians 15). Hope is one of the three great Christian virtues alongside faith and love.

The NT equivalent of shalom, eirene is not merely the absence of conflict but positive well-being and harmonious relationship. Jesus is called the 'Prince of Peace' and 'our peace' (Ephesians 2:14). The gospel is the 'gospel of peace' (Romans 10:15). Paul's letters consistently open with 'grace and peace' — the summary of the gospel's gifts.

The defining word of the gospel: salvation by grace (charis) through faith, not works (Ephesians 2:8-9). Charis is unmerited, unearned divine favor — God's love poured out on those who deserve the opposite. John 1:14-17 contrasts the law given through Moses with grace and truth that came through Jesus Christ.

Literally 'not concealed' — aletheia is the uncovering of reality as it truly is. Jesus declared himself 'the truth' (John 14:6). In Ephesians 4:15, believers are to speak 'truth in love.' The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of truth who guides into all truth (John 16:13). Truth is not merely factual but personal — embodied in Christ.

The NT's key soteriological term. God's dikaiosune is both his standard (the righteousness he demands) and his gift (the righteousness he provides in Christ). Romans 3:21-22 reveals God's righteousness 'through faith in Jesus Christ.' It is forensic (declared righteous before God) and ethical (living rightly). Matthew 5:6 calls the blessed those who hunger for it.

The NT word for holy, used of God, the Holy Spirit, Scripture, and believers. The 'Holy Spirit' (Hagion Pneuma) appears over 90 times in the NT. Believers are called 'saints' (hagioi — holy ones) — not by their perfection but by their consecration to God. 1 Peter 1:16 quotes Leviticus: 'Be holy, for I am holy.'

One of the most profound words in the NT. John 1:1 opens 'In the beginning was the Logos' — connecting Jesus to the creative word of God in Genesis and to Greek philosophical concepts of the rational principle underlying reality. The Logos is God's self-expression, creativity, and wisdom made flesh. It echoes the Hebrew dabar.

The Greek equivalent of the Hebrew ruach. The NT's teaching on the Holy Spirit (Hagion Pneuma) is built on this word. The Spirit descends at Jesus' baptism (Matthew 3:16), and fills believers at Pentecost (Acts 2). John 3 connects pneuma with spiritual rebirth. Paul teaches the Spirit's role in sanctification (Galatians 5:16-25).

The Greek equivalent of the Hebrew nephesh — the whole life and person. In Matthew 10:28, Jesus distinguishes between those who kill the body and the One who can destroy both body and soul (psuche). In John 10:11, Jesus 'lays down his psuche' for the sheep. It encompasses the emotional, volitional, and relational aspects of personhood.

definition: Life, the life of God, eternal life
extended_definition: In John's Gospel, zoe refers primarily to divine, eternal life — the very life of God shared with believers. 'I am the resurrection and the life (zoe)' (John 11:25). John 10:10 promises 'life (zoe) and have it abundantly.' This is qualitative as well as quantitative — not just endless existence but participation in God's own life.

definition: Eternal, everlasting, of the age to come
extended_definition: Often translated 'eternal' or 'everlasting,' aionios comes from aion (age). It describes the quality of life that belongs to the coming age — God's own unending life. John 17:3 defines it: 'This is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ.' It is not merely endless time but a different quality of existence.

Literally a 'change of mind' (meta = after/change, noia = mind). NT repentance is a total reorientation of one's thinking, values, and direction. John the Baptist, Jesus, and the apostles all began their preaching with calls to metanoia (Matthew 3:2; Mark 1:15; Acts 2:38). It is not mere remorse but genuine transformation of direction.

Like the Hebrew chata, hamartia originally meant to miss the target in archery. In the NT, it describes the human failure to conform to God's standard. Romans 3:23: 'All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.' John 1:29 presents Jesus as the Lamb who takes away the hamartia of the world. Paul develops sin as both acts and a reigning power.

From the marketplace and battlefield — buying back a slave or prisoner of war. Christ's redemption is the ultimate apolutrosis: releasing humanity from bondage to sin, death, and the law through his own blood (Romans 3:24; Ephesians 1:7). It echoes the Exodus and amplifies it into a cosmic liberation.

The NT equivalent of the Hebrew kabod. The doxa of God is his manifested presence and excellence. Jesus revealed the doxa of the Father (John 1:14; 17:5). The ultimate goal of salvation is the glorification of believers — sharing in God's doxa (Romans 8:30). Doxology ('glory-word') is the pattern of NT worship.

Used only in John's Gospel for the Holy Spirit (John 14:16, 26; 15:26; 16:7) and of Jesus in 1 John 2:1. Literally 'one called alongside to help.' In legal contexts, an advocate or defense attorney. The Spirit as Parakletos teaches, reminds, testifies, convicts, and guides — an ever-present helper for the believer.

The central proclamation of Jesus: 'The kingdom (basileia) of God has come near — repent and believe!' (Mark 1:15). The basileia is both present (in Jesus' ministry) and future (at his return). It is wherever God's reign is acknowledged and exercised. The Sermon on the Mount describes the ethics of kingdom life.

Applied to both God the Father and Jesus the Son in the NT. Luke 2:11 announces the birth of 'a Savior, who is Christ the Lord.' A title of honor used for rulers in the Greco-Roman world, but the NT reserves its deepest meaning for Christ who saves from sin and death. Titus 2:13 calls him 'our great God and Savior Jesus Christ.'

The comprehensive term for God's saving work in Christ. In Luke 19:9, Jesus declares 'salvation (soteria) has come to this house.' Romans 1:16 calls the gospel 'the power of God for salvation.' Soteria encompasses past (justification), present (sanctification), and future (glorification) dimensions of rescue from sin's penalty, power, and presence.

Literally 'the called-out ones' — those summoned out of the world to belong to God. Jesus declares he will build his ekklesia (Matthew 16:18). In Acts, the ekklesia is the community of believers in each city. Paul teaches that the ekklesia is the body of Christ (Ephesians 1:22-23). It existed before the word 'Christian' was coined.

In the NT, nomos primarily refers to the Mosaic Law (Torah). Paul's complex theology of law includes: the law reveals sin (Romans 3:20), cannot justify (Galatians 2:16), but is holy and good (Romans 7:12). Christ is the 'end' (telos) of the law (Romans 10:4) — fulfilling its purpose. The law of Christ is the new covenant expression of God's will.

The root of English 'dynamic' and 'dynamite.' In Acts 1:8, Jesus promises the disciples will receive dunamis when the Holy Spirit comes. Paul proclaims the gospel is God's dunamis for salvation (Romans 1:16). Miracles are 'works of power' (dynameis). The resurrection demonstrates God's ultimate dunamis over death.

definition: Heart, the inner life, the center of the person
extended_definition: Like the Hebrew leb, the kardia is the center of the whole person — thought, will, emotion, and moral life. Jesus teaches that sin originates in the heart (Matthew 15:19). God searches the heart (Romans 8:27). The new covenant promise is a new heart (Ezekiel 36:26), fulfilled through the Spirit. Love God with all your kardia (Matthew 22:37).

definition: To repent, to change one's mind, to turn
extended_definition: The verb form of metanoia — the act of repenting. John the Baptist's first message: 'Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.' Jesus repeats it in Mark 1:15. Repentance is not a one-time event but an ongoing disposition of the believer. Acts 2:38 calls for baptism as the outward sign of inward metanoia.

Literally 'good message' — the announcement of the best news in history. Mark 1:1 opens: 'The beginning of the gospel (euangelion) of Jesus Christ.' Paul summarizes it in 1 Corinthians 15:1-4: Christ died for sins, was buried, and rose again. The euangelion is not advice or a suggestion but a royal announcement of what God has done in Christ.

From telos (end, goal), teleios describes that which has reached its intended end or purpose. Matthew 5:48 calls believers to be teleios as their heavenly Father is. It does not primarily mean sinless perfection but wholeness, maturity, and completeness. James uses it of the mature believer who endures testing (James 1:4).

definition: To remain, abide, stay, continue, dwell
extended_definition: A key word in John's Gospel and Epistles. Jesus calls disciples to 'abide' (meno) in him as branches in the vine (John 15:1-11). Those who meno in Christ bear much fruit. 1 John uses it repeatedly for the mutual indwelling of God and believers. It describes a permanent, active, relational dwelling — not mere static existence.

definition: Prophet, one who speaks forth, foreteller
extended_definition: A prophetes is not primarily a foreteller of the future but a forth-teller of God's word — one who speaks on God's behalf. Prophets in both testaments call people back to covenant faithfulness. Jesus is recognized as a prophet (Luke 7:16) and is also the Prophet like Moses (Acts 3:22). Paul lists prophecy as a key spiritual gift (1 Corinthians 14).

definition: Mystery, secret, hidden truth now revealed
extended_definition: In the NT, musterion is not something permanently unknowable but a truth formerly hidden and now revealed in Christ. Ephesians 3:3-6 describes the mystery: Gentiles are co-heirs with Israel in Christ. Colossians 1:26-27 names the mystery: 'Christ in you, the hope of glory.' Revelation is the unveiling of God's mysteries.

Literally 'one sent out' — a commissioned representative. Jesus chose twelve apostles as the foundation of his new covenant community (Ephesians 2:20). Paul defends his apostleship vigorously (Galatians 1:1; 1 Corinthians 9:1). The apostles were eyewitnesses of the resurrection (Acts 1:22) and the primary transmitters of the gospel.

Used in the Greco-Roman world for the official visit of a king or emperor. In the NT, parousia refers primarily to the second coming of Christ (Matthew 24:3; 1 Thessalonians 4:15). It conveys both arrival and presence — Christ's return will be visible, glorious, and transformative. The church lives in anticipation of the parousia.

The NT equivalent of hesed — covenant mercy and compassion. 'Lord, have mercy' (Kyrie eleison) is the most ancient Christian prayer. Luke 18:13 captures it in the publican's prayer. God is 'rich in mercy' (Ephesians 2:4). James 2:13 declares mercy triumphs over judgment. Eleos motivates the care of the vulnerable.

definition: Flesh, human nature, body, sinful nature
extended_definition: Sarx has a range of meaning: physical flesh/body (John 1:14 — 'the Word became flesh'), human nature in its weakness (Matthew 26:41 — 'the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak'), and sinful human nature in opposition to the Spirit (Romans 8:5-8; Galatians 5:17-21). Context determines which sense is intended.

definition: Age, era, eternity, world, course of time
extended_definition: Refers to a period of time with its own character and governing powers. The NT speaks of 'this age' (characterized by sin, Satan's influence, and mortality) and 'the age to come' (the kingdom of God in its fullness). The two ages overlap in Christ's resurrection — believers live 'between the ages.' 'Forever' is often eis tous aionas ton aionon ('unto the ages of ages').

The removal of enmity between God and humanity through Christ's atoning work. Romans 5:10-11 and 2 Corinthians 5:18-20 develop this concept. God initiated the reconciliation while we were still enemies — an act of unilateral grace. The church is given a 'ministry of reconciliation' — announcing what God has accomplished.

The ritual immersion that marks entry into the Christian community. Jesus was baptized to 'fulfill all righteousness' (Matthew 3:15). Acts 2:38 connects baptism to repentance and the gift of the Spirit. Romans 6:3-4 interprets baptism as union with Christ's death and resurrection — dying to the old life, rising to the new.

The faculty of rational thought and moral perception. Romans 12:2 calls for the 'renewal of the mind (nous)' — transformation from within rather than conformity to the world. 1 Corinthians 2:16 declares that believers have 'the mind of Christ.' Spiritual discernment and right worship engage the nous (1 Corinthians 14:15).
